item.title: Canada makes rural immigration programme permanent
item.description: By Favour Ulebor Canada has made its Rural Community Immigration Pilot a permanent programme to attract and retain skilled foreign workers in smaller communities facing persistent labour shortages. The Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship, Lena Metlege Diab, announced the decision on Monday, November 9, 2026, in Pictou County, Nova Scotia. According to a statement published on the website of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC), the programme will initially retain the 14 communities currently participating in the pilot, with plans to expand to more communities in the future. The employer- and community-driven programme is designed to address labour shortages in rural areas by connecting skilled foreign workers and their families with employers and community support services. It also seeks to encourage newcomers to settle permanently in smaller communities and contribute to their economic development. Speaking during the announcement, Diab said the government recognised the critical role rural communities played in Canada’s economy despite the challenges they faced in attracting workers. “Our government understands that rural communities play a critical role in powering Canada’s economy. At the same time, many face real challenges finding the workers they need. “That’s why we’re transitioning our successful rural immigration pilot into a permanent program—helping smaller communities attract and retain essential workers who deliver services and drive economic growth. “We appreciate that a one-size-fits-all approach to immigration doesn’t work for rural Canada, and this permanent pathway is one part of our work to ensure that communities of all sizes can share in the benefits of responsible, sustainable immigration,” she said. Under Canada’s 2027–2029 Immigration Levels Plan, the government has allocated 5,500 admission spaces to the permanent Rural Community Immigration Program. The government said the initiative was part of its broader immigration policy aimed at stabilising the number of immigrants admitted into the country, reducing the temporary resident population and retaining skilled foreign workers already contributing to local communities. It added that preliminary results from the pilot showed that foreign workers had helped address labour shortages in critical sectors, including healthcare, education, sales and services, between 2025 and 2026. The department also disclosed that participating communities had vetted and designated more than 1,950 trusted employers experiencing persistent labour shortages that could not be addressed through the local workforce between January 2025 and August 2026. The transition to a permanent programme is expected to provide rural employers with a more reliable supply of skilled foreign workers while supporting the long-term economic development of participating communities. item.title: I’m a godfather, but I don’t impose appointments on governors — Osoba
item.description: By Efe Onodjae Former Ogun State Governor, Olusegun Osoba has defended the role of political godfathers in Nigeria’s democracy, saying their responsibility should be to offer advice and guidance rather than impose political appointees on elected governors. Osoba, who spoke during a podcast hosted by Reuben Abati and shared on X (formerly Twitter), said he considered himself a political godfather but had deliberately avoided interfering in the administration of his political successors. According to him, he had never nominated anyone for appointment as commissioner, special adviser, councillor or local government chairman in the state. He said: “I agree, I’m a godfather. But one thing that is working for me in my state is that I hardly interfere. I counsel and advise him. I have never nominated one person into his government.” Explaining his position, the former governor said imposing candidates on an administration could undermine the governor’s authority and create unnecessary divisions among his political supporters. He noted that appointing one person from the numerous people around him could offend others, while anyone recommended by him might be viewed with suspicion within the administration. Osoba recalled that during his tenure as governor, he adopted a system that allowed each federal constituency to nominate candidates for commissioner positions. He said he requested one name from each federal constituency and subsequently reviewed their credentials before assigning them portfolios, adding that the approach helped him avoid pressure from political associates. The former governor maintained that political godfathers should ensure that people who worked for a candidate during electioneering campaigns were recognised and compensated, but should not dictate how an elected governor runs his administration. “That’s the role of a godfather. I agree, I’m a godfather,” he said. Osoba also defended the participation of experienced elders in candidate selection, citing his support for a presidential candidate whom he described as experienced, having served in the Lagos State House of Assembly, House of Representatives and Senate, as well as in the corporate sector. item.title: Charlie Kirk murder trial set for June 2028, suspect faces death penalty
item.description: The trial of the man accused of murdering US conservative firebrand Charlie Kirk will begin in June 2028, the judge said Monday. “Jury selection will begin June 21, 2028,” judge Tony Graf told the Utah district court, noting that 105 days have been reserved for the trial. Tyler Robinson, 23, faces a potential death penalty for allegedly killing Kirk with a gunshot to the neck on a university campus in the western US state of Utah on September 10, 2025. The killing of Kirk at age 31 at an event planned by his right-wing youth organization, Turning Point, sent shockwaves through the US political world. Kirk had become a popular leader in a Christian Nationalist movement that preaches traditional values while voicing intolerance for diversity and LGBTQ communities. Turning Point was key to mobilizing youth support for Donald Trump’s re-election as president in 2024. The group is now led by his wife, Erika Kirk. The prosecution had sought a trial as early as January 2028, while Robinson’s lawyers had wanted until the end of 2029 to prepare their defense. Last month, Trump criticized the judge and said the case “should be tried within a month, not three years.” Kirk’s assassination last year triggered a 33-hour manhunt culminating in Robinson surrendering to authorities. He has pled not guilty. The prosecution has presented text messages in which Robinson confessed to planning the murder to his roommate, a transgender person with whom they allege Robinson was in a relationship. The defense has focused on alleged weaknesses in the DNA and ballistic evidence. What I want to defeat is poverty and insecurity. “But to defeat that, you need to defeat ignorance in people going to just vote based on sentiment or looking for something,” Adebayo said. “You also have to defeat lethargy where people get tired, ‘Oh, my vote doesn’t count. item.title: Manchester United are becoming a club of survival rather than ambition
item.description: The 4-4 draw against Aston Villa felt like a victory at Old Trafford, but the fact that supporters could celebrate a point while their club sits in the relegation zone tells a more troubling story about how far United’s expectations have fallen. There was a time when a draw at Old Trafford felt like a defeat. Manchester United were a club built around winning, where anything short of three points could leave supporters disappointed, regardless of the performance. The expectation was not simply to compete but to dominate, to set the standards and to make winning feel like an obligation. Those expectations seem increasingly distant. On Sunday, Manchester United celebrated a 4-4 draw against Aston Villa with the sort of emotion usually reserved for a significant victory. Two goals in stoppage time, courtesy of Joshua Zirkzee and Patrick Dorgu, rescued a point after Michael Carrick’s side had twice fallen two goals behind. The comeback was extraordinary, the atmosphere was electric and the players had every reason to appreciate their resilience. But perhaps the most revealing aspect of the afternoon was not the comeback itself. It was how much it meant. Manchester United are now in a position where avoiding defeat feels like an achievement. A point against Aston Villa, under ordinary circumstances, would hardly have been considered a successful afternoon for a club of United’s stature. Yet the circumstances have become so desperate that the draw felt like a victory. That is how quickly footballing standards can collapse. United sit 18th in the Premier League with eight points from 10 matches . They have managed just one league victory, recorded against Ipswich Town in August, and Sunday’s result extended their winless league run to eight matches. It is a club-record sequence in the Premier League. The numbers are alarming, but the deeper concern is what they reveal about the club’s changing relationship with success. Manchester United have become a team defined by what they are trying to avoid rather than what they are trying to achieve. There was the determination to fight back, the willingness to keep attacking and the refusal to surrender even when the game appeared beyond them. Instead of discussing title challenges, European qualification or the development of a convincing footballing identity, the conversation increasingly revolves around managerial uncertainty, defensive mistakes, relegation calculations and the possibility of another disappointing weekend. Survival has become the immediate ambition. And that is a remarkable development for a club whose history was built on refusing to accept anything less than excellence. Sunday’s performance captured both sides of United’s current identity. There was the determination to fight back, the willingness to keep attacking and the refusal to surrender even when the game appeared beyond them. Coming back from 2-0 down, reaching 2-2, falling behind again and eventually recovering from 4-2 demonstrated a spirit that supporters have desperately wanted to see. However, resilience cannot become an excuse for repeated carelessness. United conceded twice inside the opening four minutes. They then surrendered their defensive organisation again immediately after half-time, allowing John McGinn to score from the penalty spot before Leon Goretzka extended Villa’s advantage. The attacking response was admirable, but the defensive problems that made such a dramatic recovery necessary were equally concerning. There is a difference between fighting back from adversity and repeatedly creating adversity for yourself. For Carrick, the challenge is no longer simply convincing supporters that his team can produce entertaining football. He must demonstrate that Manchester United can become dependable again. The occasional spectacular comeback cannot compensate for a team that struggles to manage the opening minutes of matches, protect advantages or maintain concentration. There is also a wider question about the club’s direction. Manchester United’s problems cannot be reduced to one manager, one transfer window or one poor run of results. The instability surrounding the club has created an environment in which every setback becomes another argument about leadership, recruitment and the footballing structure. The manager becomes the immediate subject of scrutiny, but the problems appear considerably deeper. The danger is that United become accustomed to this existence. When a club repeatedly lowers its expectations to accommodate its circumstances, mediocrity can gradually become normal. Supporters who once demanded victories begin celebrating draws. A team that once approached matches expecting to dictate proceedings now approaches them hoping to survive the next defensive crisis. That is perhaps the most disturbing part of United’s current predicament. The 4-4 draw against Aston Villa should not be dismissed. There was genuine character in the comeback, and the players deserved credit for refusing to surrender. Football supporters should be allowed to enjoy extraordinary moments, even in difficult seasons. But one dramatic afternoon cannot disguise a deeply troubling campaign. Manchester United have spent years searching for a return to the standards that made them one of football’s most formidable institutions. Now, with the relegation zone beneath their feet, the immediate concern is no longer how quickly they can return to the summit but whether they can first escape the bottom three. A draw that once would have been considered two points dropped has become a reason for celebration. Perhaps that is the clearest indication of how far Manchester United have fallen. The problem is no longer just that United are struggling to win football matches . It is that a club built on ambition is beginning to look increasingly comfortable with survival. item.title: UK man convicted of fraud for secretly working five government jobs at once
item.description: A 56-year-old civil servant in the United Kingdom, UK, Kashim Chowdhury has been convicted of nine counts of fraud after secretly holding multiple full-time government jobs and fraudulently earning more than £284,000 in taxpayers’ money. Chowdhury, from east London, held five overlapping government positions in the spring of 2023, concealing his multiple employment arrangements from the departments that hired him. After seven hours of deliberation, a jury unanimously found him guilty of eight counts of fraud by false representation and one count of fraud by failure to disclose. The prosecution accused Chowdhury of “deliberate, intentional dishonesty” and “exploiting the system” to secure multiple salaries from public sector employers. During the proceedings, the judge said Chowdhury faced a “very significant custodial sentence”. He also refused him bail, citing the seriousness of the offences and Chowdhury’s own wellbeing. Sarah Melo, a specialist prosecutor at the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) Serious Economic Organised Crime and International Directorate, described his actions as sustained dishonesty. “This was sustained and deliberate dishonesty,” Melo said. “He knew he could not legitimately hold multiple full-time positions at the same time, but continued to conceal what he was doing.” A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said Chowdhury had “abused the trust placed in him as a public servant”. The department added that it would use all available avenues to recover the proceeds of his offending. Between 2020 and 2023, Chowdhury held eight overlapping full-time public sector positions and earned a total of £350,000, according to evidence presented in court. Prosecutors told the court that he provided inaccurate information about his employment status on job application forms and failed to disclose to government departments that he was already employed as a civil servant. After securing the positions, he also failed to inform his employers that he was working for other government departments. Chowdhury was permitted to work entirely from home after telling his employers he was caring for his mother, with whom he lived in east London. His mother had dementia and was diagnosed with terminal cancer in 2023. However, rather than reduce his workload to care for her, he continued taking on additional government positions. In the spring of 2023, he held positions across the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, the Department of Health and Social Care, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), the Department for Business and Trade, the Food Standards Agency and the Home Office. During the period, he was contracted to work 183 hours a week, exceeding the total number of hours available in seven days. item.title: Full list: Canada lists foreigners eligible for rural permanent residence
item.description: Canada has outlined six eligibility requirements for foreign nationals seeking permanent residence through its Rural Community Immigration Program, a pathway designed to attract skilled immigrants to participating rural communities across the country. The programme offers permanent residence to eligible foreigners who want to work and settle in selected Canadian communities, particularly areas seeking skilled migrants to fill positions that cannot be filled by local residents. According to Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC), participating communities will approve designated employers to recruit skilled foreign nationals for available positions. To qualify for permanent residence under the programme, applicants must obtain a valid recommendation certificate from a participating community and secure a valid job offer from a designated employer within that community. They must also have at least one year, equivalent to 1,560 hours, of related work experience within the previous three years. Other requirements include demonstrating language proficiency through an approved test, possessing a Canadian educational credential or its foreign equivalent, and providing proof of sufficient funds to support themselves and their families. Full list of eligibility requirements According to IRCC, foreigners seeking permanent residence through the programme must meet the following six requirements: Community recommendation: Obtain a valid recommendation certificate from a participating community in Canada. Valid job offer: Secure a valid job offer from a designated employer within the participating community. Work experience: Have at least one year (1,560 hours) of related work experience within the past three years. Language proficiency: Demonstrate English or French language ability by taking an approved language test. Educational qualification: Possess a Canadian educational credential or a foreign equivalent. Proof of funds: Provide evidence of having sufficient money to support themselves and their families after arriving in Canada. The programme is designed to help participating rural communities attract skilled foreign nationals while providing immigrants with an opportunity to obtain permanent residence and establish themselves in Canada. Applicants are required to satisfy the eligibility conditions and secure the necessary community recommendation and employment offer before applying for permanent residence. The response is evidence-led investigation, completed corrective action and stronger preventive controls. “1,609,553 records have been removed, comprising 1,608,660 confirmed invalid registrations and 873 verified deceased-voter records. INEC noted that while the recent 2025/2026 CVR clean-up resolved immediate anomalies, historical data carried over from 2011 to 2023 continues to present legacy duplications. Consequently, the commission’s board has directed that flagged entries from past cycles be expunged after verification. To further safeguard the integrity of the upcoming 2027 polls, INEC assured the public that robust mechanisms—including the mandatory physical presence of voters and biometric authentication via the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) using fingerprints or facial recognition—remain firmly in place to prevent multiple voting and unauthorized accreditation.
